### [58] [When Local Definitions Are Missing: Stable Errors in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15597)
*Zengqing Wu,Chuan Xiao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Contracts, technical manuals, and online communities often give familiar words special meanings and define them in one place. A language model that reads a passage without that definition may use the usual meaning and give an answer that sounds right but is wrong. We study this with multiple-choice questions whose correct answers depend on a local definition. The questions come from a synthetic vocabulary, commercial contracts, Reddit community glossaries, and the documentation of a decentralized exchange. We ask three language models each question with and without the definition. Without using the answer key, we then test whether their repeated answers and stated confidence reveal their own errors. Separately, we give a small open model the answer key and test whether it can predict which questions larger models get wrong. We report three findings. (1) Familiar words that a source redefines cause the most errors. Models often repeat the same wrong answer, and neither repeated answers nor stated confidence reliably flag it. (2) The source definition fixes most errors on synthetic questions, but a definition drawn from the model's own prior knowledge does not. In real contracts, the source definition fixes only about half of the errors. (3) Given an answer key, a small model can rank questions by how likely larger models are to get them wrong. These results call for tests that check answers against the full source, including its local definitions.

### [59] [ChJGBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Chinese Legal Judgment Generation with Diagnostic Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15639)
*Yinghao Hu,Linggang Kong,Qian Xiao,Yuting Huang,Yunlong Zhang,Yujie Zhang,Yiquan Wu,Fei Duan,Kaisong Song,Jun Lin,Kun Kuang,Fei Wu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: With the rapid development of LLMs, increasing attention has been paid to whether they can reliably generate complete and legally valid judicial documents. This calls for a benchmark capable of evaluating whether models can accurately apply statutes and resolve outcome-critical issues, including claims, charges, penalties, and monetary obligations. However, existing benchmarks typically focus on isolated legal tasks or coarse-grained evaluation. We introduce ChJGBench, a benchmark for generating the reasoning and dispositive sections of Chinese judgments across civil, criminal, and administrative cases. Built from 3,462 real-world judgments, ChJGBench provides a case-type-aware diagnostic evaluation framework comprising 13 metric types and adopts a hybrid paradigm. Experiments reveal no uniform advantage for legal-domain models over general-purpose models, with model strengths varying across diagnostic dimensions. Performance is generally stronger on criminal cases, while civil and administrative cases continue to present substantial challenges.

Abstract: With the rapid development of LLMs, increasing attention has been paid to whether they can reliably generate complete and legally valid judicial documents. This calls for a benchmark capable of evaluating whether models can accurately apply statutes and resolve outcome-critical issues, including claims, charges, penalties, and monetary obligations. However, existing benchmarks typically focus on isolated legal tasks or coarse-grained evaluation. We introduce ChJGBench, a benchmark for generating the reasoning and dispositive sections of Chinese judgments across civil, criminal, and administrative cases. Built from 3,462 real-world judgments, ChJGBench provides a case-type-aware diagnostic evaluation framework comprising 13 metric types and adopts a hybrid paradigm. Experiments reveal no uniform advantage for legal-domain models over general-purpose models, with model strengths varying across diagnostic dimensions. Performance is generally stronger on criminal cases, while civil and administrative cases continue to present substantial challenges.

### [60] [Differential Backpack Language Models: Sense Inhibition via Signed Contextualization Weights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15642)
*Konstantinos Skianis,Giannis Nikolentzos,Polykarpos Meladianos,Michalis Vazirgiannis*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Backpack language models predict with a strictly linear combination of non-contextual per-word sense vectors, weighted by non-negative contextualization scores. We show that non-negativity conflates two properties: the linear readout, which carries the interpretability, and the conic combination, which merely restricts it. We relax the latter by computing the sense weights with differential attention, a difference of two softmax maps with a learned per-sense gain, so context can actively inhibit a sense; we call the result a differential Backpack. At equal parameters on WikiText-103 this cuts the Backpack's perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31%, improves over the softmax Backpack at every sense count, persists with a shrinking margin up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText, and is localized at the sense layer by ablations and controls. The learned inhibition is directly interpretable (a financial context drives the river sense of bank to -0.50), and the preserved per-sense attribution predicts counterfactual removals exactly. We tested a number of combination rules, showing the linear interface is nearly free. Making the readout nonlinear gains only 0.43 perplexity points while invalidating two thirds of the decomposition. The differential Backpack's senses are also better representations, improving zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%.

### [61] [Can Agents Relive Past Experiences? Diagnosing Event-Affect Decoupling in Affective-Episodic Retrospection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15655)
*Tingna Xie,Ming Wang,Shi Feng,Yongkang Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: As memory-augmented agents increasingly support long-term and personalized interactions, reliable recall of emotional experiences while preserving their associated affect becomes necessary. However, existing evaluations usually assess emotion accuracy and factual memory grounding separately, overlooking event-affect correspondence. In this work, we formulate Affective-Episodic Retrospection (AER) as a task that explicitly evaluates the recovery of past events, associated affects, and their correspondence, and define Event-Affect Decoupling as a failure mode where the correct emotion is recalled but associated with the wrong episode. To diagnose Event-Affect Decoupling, we propose EM-TRACE, a stage-wise framework that decomposes AER into retrieval, affect recovery, and realization. On a controlled GoEmotions-based benchmark, Emotion-only retrieval achieves 28.65% affect recovery but retrieves the target episode for only 4.44% of queries, yielding a UAR of 24.21%. Further analysis reveals that event retrieval and affect assignment introduce distinct binding failures. These findings show that reliable AER requires grounded recall of emotional experiences, where episode retrieval, affect recovery, event-affect binding, and generation quality should be evaluated jointly. Our code is available at this https URL .

### [62] [ALMeD: Medieval French Gold-Standard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15661)
*Ragini Menon,Sabine Tittel*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Medieval French is one of the Romance vernacular languages with a significant history of transmission and an enormous influence on other vernacular languages of the time. The sources convey valuable knowledge about all aspects of culture. The study of Medieval French has, over the last few years, increasingly benefited from NLP-based methods. There have been numerous efforts to parse medieval French; however, these efforts use corpora comprising legal texts and -- primarily -- literary texts as their foundation and training data. This means that, except for juridical resources, scientific literature is overlooked. We present ALMeD, an annotated, semantically rich corpus (work-in-progress) of medical and surgical treatises produced in medieval French, i.e., Old and Middle French, including Anglo-Norman. Our semantically disambiguated gold standard goes beyond existing resources, focusing on medical terminology, and accounts for morphological development, evolving syntactical structures and the lack of spelling normalisation in these languages.

### [63] [Dynamic Block-Online Streaming ASR for Low-Resource Agglutinative Code-Switching Speech with Morphology-Aware Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15691)
*Kazi Rafat,Afifa Imran,Md. Ismail Hossain,Md. Romzan Ali,Fuad Rahman,Sifat Momen,Shafin Rahman,Nabeel Mohammed*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Low-resource, agglutinative languages challenge low-latency ASR, as fixed lookahead windows fail when grapheme order diverges, suffixes cross code-switch boundaries, or code-switching data is imbalanced. We present the first comprehensive study of streaming ASR for intra-sentential Bangla-English code-switching, identifying a mismatch between strict causal streaming and long-range morphological dependencies. We introduce a Dynamic Block-Online framework with VAD-aligned inference that balances semantics, latency, and context, enabling global bidirectional attention to preserve morphological integrity. To mitigate data scarcity, we propose Script-Anchored Loanword Injection, augmenting training text with English loanwords to model phonotactic transitions. We introduce CS-WER to diagnose switch, root, and suffix errors, and show that flexible latency budgets enhance recognition of agglutinative and mixed-language speech, with successful transfer to menstrual-medical domains.

### [64] [Computational Explanations of Semantic Universals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15804)
*Shane Steinert-Threlkeld,Jakub Szymanik*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Despite their differences, the languages of the world share many deep features when it comes to how they express meaning. These semantic universals are likely to reflect shared aspects of human cognitive, communicative, and social structure. Recent advances in cross-linguistic semantics and computational linguistics allow us to develop explanations of the sources of such properties. This Element presents a body of work doing just that: we explicate a framework for providing computational explanations of semantic universals and then describe several such explanations using principles of ease of learning and efficient communication. Empirical domains include quantifiers, color terms, modals, and indefinites. After providing these explanations, we provide a discussion of future directions for advancing the explanatory power of computational methods in semantic typology.

### [65] [Is Spoken Hungarian Low-resource?: A Quantitative Survey of Hungarian Speech Data Sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15961)
*Péter Mihajlik,Katalin Mády,Anna Kohári,Fruzsina Sára Vargha,Gábor Kiss,Tekla Etelka Gráczi,A. Seza Doğruöz*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Even though various speech data sets are available in Hungarian, there is a lack of a general overview about their types and sizes. To fill in this gap, we provide a survey of available data sets in spoken Hungarian in five categories (e.g., monolingual, Hungarian part of multilingual, pathological, child-related and dialectal collections). In total, the estimated size of available data is about 2800 hours (across 7500 speakers) and it represents a rich spoken language diversity. However, the distribution of the data and its alignment to real-life (e.g. speech recognition) tasks is far from optimal indicating the need for additional larger-scale natural language speech data sets. Our survey presents an overview of available data sets for Hungarian explaining their strengths and weaknesses which is useful for researchers working on Hungarian across disciplines. In addition, our survey serves as a starting point towards a unified foundational speech model specific to Hungarian.

### [66] [Better Boundary Prediction Does Not Guarantee Better Structural Representation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15971)
*Michael Zhou,Markus Frohmann,Junghyun Min,En-Shiun Annie Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Punctuation marks often mark phrase boundaries, carrying linguistic information. Therefore, punctuation marks' abundance and feasibility as proxies of linguistic structure has led to suggestions that using punctuation marks to optimise on phrasal structure may help language models (LMs) improve their representations of argument, semantic, and syntactic structures. In this paper, we test the above claim in English across three primary LM architectures: decoder-only, encoder-only, and encoder-decoder LMs, by complementing traditional token prediction with punctuation restoration (PR). Our evidence, collected at the <1B parameter scale, suggests that optimising for boundary prediction does not necessarily guarantee higher-quality structural representation in decoder-only, encoder-decoder, and encoder-only LMs, failing to improve performance on downstream tasks that require understanding structure in linguistic input.

### [67] [Human-Likeness and Conversational Preference Diverge for Synthesized Agent Speech in Customer-Service Calls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16051)
*Jeffrey M. Girard,Antony D'Avirro,Jason Z. Zheng,Jacqueline R. Vertino,Benjamin Peloquin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Listeners can judge an agent's speech on how human it sounds (human-likeness) and on how much they would want to talk to it (conversational preference). Listening tests rarely ask about conversational preference, so the relation between the two judgments is unclear. We compared them in paired-choice tests on 120 turns that actors improvised as customer-service representatives. On each trial, two agents spoke the same turn. In Study 1, both agents came from six commercial text-to-speech systems, each with eight voices. In Study 2, one was the actor's original recording and the other a system. Some systems ranked higher on human-likeness, and others on conversational preference. Listeners chose systems over actors in 19% of human-likeness trials but 36% of conversational preference trials (and 49% for the most preferred system). On both judgments, variation among a system's voices was about three-quarters of that between systems. Of three automatic naturalness scores, two predicted lower human-likeness, and none predicted conversational preference. In this setting, listeners tended to favor faster speech and fewer pauses between clauses on both judgments, and more pitch variation for conversational preference. Thus, measuring only human-likeness or testing one voice per system can misjudge which agents listeners would rather talk to.

### [68] [Privileged Information Does Not Guarantee Privileged Guidance: Auditing On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16064)
*Haoyi Qiu,Akshat Agarwal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on next-token targets from a teacher, a frozen copy of the student that additionally receives privileged information, such as a worked solution, hidden from the student. Whether student gains reflect that information remains unclear. Taking the worked solution as privileged information, we audit four stages across three Qwen3 scales on mathematics: Source, whether the teacher can use the solution; Encoding, whether the resulting token targets are useful; Transmission, whether the student learns from the targets; and Expression, whether the student applies the learned behavior without the solution. With the solution, the teacher solves hard problems and recovers from student errors, yet the teacher does not reliably recognize errors, and its token targets do not favor correct trajectories. Repeated training makes successes within the student's reach more frequent rather than unlocking new ones, and corrections the student learns to predict are not reliably expressed in free generation. To isolate the solution's contribution, we vary its availability separately from teacher and student thinking modes. The largest gains occur when a teacher in thinking mode supervises a student trained and evaluated without an explicit thinking trace, and problem-only teachers often match or exceed privileged-solution teachers: the gain tracks the teacher's thinking mode rather than the solution, a pattern we call reasoning arbitrage. Accuracy gains alone therefore do not establish transfer of reasoning from privileged solutions: bottlenecks lie after Source, across Encoding, Transmission, and Expression. Future evaluations must measure what the solution adds to otherwise identical training.

### [69] [We Are What We Remember: Mental-State-Driven Memory for Long-Term Character Dialogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16223)
*Zhicheng Jia,Shuchen Wu,Zhuoshi Tong,Haisen Liao,Sicheng Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at this https URL .

### [70] [Low Language Transfer Speech-to-Text](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16260)
*Husein Zolkepli*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A multilingual speech recogniser has heard much speech in its own languages. We ask how much of that it brings to a language it was never trained on, when it is fine-tuned on the little that language has. We score 28 open multilingual models untouched on Low-Language-TTS, 50 low-resource languages in 11 writing systems, and fine-tune 24 of them on at most 1,000 clips a language, 82 hours in all, with a dev set choosing every epoch. Fine-tuning lowers every model's macro character error rate (CER), by 16.6 to 53.1 points, to 9.5 at best, and a word language model takes three CTC models 1.2 to 1.4 points lower; WER is still 34.4 at best. On the 12 languages that no model lists, every model starts at 46 or worse and the best ends at 11.7. The same architectures from random weights stay 60 points or more behind, so the gain is transfer, and an encoder left untouched already gives a Whisper or Qwen decoder most of what it needs. It is the language, not the corpus: on FLEURS recordings that ours do not share, the median model keeps 79% of its gain. It costs the languages the models knew, 5.7 points of CER on English, Spanish, French and German in the median model. Low-rank adapters on 4% of the weights come within 1.1 points of tuning everything, and on 2 of 3 models forget less. Seq2seq and language-model decoders are done within three to five epochs, while a new CTC head is still improving at twenty or thirty. Data beats epochs: 25 clips a language take Qwen3-ASR 0.6B from 60.9 to 39.3, and at equal clips presented, ten times the data is worth 9.7 points. A model that first learned forty of the languages learns the other ten no faster. On a public Malay benchmark, untouched Whisper large-v3 scores 8.9 when it detects the language and 14.9 when told the clip is Malay, because it then translates the English that speakers mix in; trained on the Scicom telephony dataset it scores 6.0.

### [71] [From Large Language Models to Efficient System One Models via Adaptive Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16321)
*Minh-Anh Nguyen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Transferring LLMs into System One decision models typically replaces the language modeling head with a decision head while retaining the full backbone, making every decision pay for all layers. Yet it remains unclear how much depth such decisions require. We find that decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers, with early layers building essential features and the final six layers removable without loss, while independently trained smaller models largely mimic the full model rather than developing specialized decision capabilities. These findings suggest that efficiency requires not simply smaller backbones, but shared computation across different depths. Building on this, we propose \method{}, which jointly trains a full model with prefix sub-models that share its final layers and decision head through self-distillation. A lightweight gate reads the hidden state at each exit to determine whether additional computation is needed, allowing one model to operate at multiple layers. Across seven decision benchmarks, our approach matches or outperforms independently trained models at every depth, while achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs through adaptive computation.

### [72] [IsharaBART: An efficient BART-Based Framework for Low-Resource Bangla Sign Language Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16359)
*Aonmoy Das,Ananna Dev Aishi,Md. Fazlul Kader*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Millions of Bangla Sign Language (BdSL) users lack reliable automatic translation tools. Existing systems are limited by data scarcity, unidirectional design, and computationally expensive architectures that are not suitable for low-resource deployment. We introduce IsharaBART, a bidirectional generative framework for gloss-sentence translation in BdSL. IsharaBART uses Bidirectional and Auto-Regressive Transformers (BART)-based conditional language modeling with denoising learning objectives. We developed a parallel dataset of 1,000 professionally annotated gloss-sentence pairs, balanced across tenses and structures. We expanded the dataset to 4,831 pairs through four augmentation techniques: rule-based tense transformations, masked token substitutions, back-translation, and one-shot prompting. A compact denoising sequence-to-sequence model was pre-trained from scratch on monolingual Bangla text from six different corpora, then fine-tuned on the annotated and augmented datasets. We compare IsharaBART against four larger baseline models under identical conditions, where it achieves comparable or superior bidirectional performance. On the gloss-to-sentence (G2S) task, it attains Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU-4) score up to 51.7, and on the sentence-to-gloss (S2G) task, it achieves 61.40, outperforming multilingual models despite having fewer than 10% of the parameters. Ablation studies demonstrate that pre-training provides 62.5-90.4% faster convergence and 11.5-118% higher BLEU-4 than scratch. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces trainable parameters by 99.3%, but with 28.0-52.2% loss of BLEU-4 compared to full-parameter fine-tuning.

### [73] [Saidzoda-Kazakh-EmbeddingGemma-300M: How Far One Epoch of Generated Questions Takes a Small Kazakh Embedder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16399)
*Tohir Saidzoda,Madina Abdusalomzoda,Abubakr Abdullozoda,Amin Jalilov,Faroiz Bobokhon,Aibek Shokanuly*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EmbeddingGemma-300M is a small open embedder, and used as released it finds the right passage first for 60.8% of the Kazakh Belebele retrieval questions. We present Saidzoda-Kazakh-EmbeddingGemma-300M, the same model fully fine-tuned for one epoch on 208,511 pairs: 166,263 Kazakh questions that our own language model wrote about source passages from encyclopedias, Wikipedia, news and books, each checked by a second model, plus English and Russian replay. On Kazakh Belebele, recall@1 rises from 60.8% to 78.0% and recall@10 from 76.3% to 91.4%. Our model scores above 161 of the 194 models with a published MTEB score on the same test, among them OpenAI text-embedding-3-large (47.1%). The other 33 score higher: the ten best are large multi-billion-parameter or closed models, reaching up to 92.2%, and at least 9 are open models of up to 0.6B parameters, the smallest with 339M. We also scored 6 Kazakh-specific embedders shared on Hugging Face with the same code in one run: our model (77.3% there) is ahead of 4 of them, including the two E5-base models of similar size (72.6% and 69.0%), and behind kaz-embedder (86.0%, three towers with 1,695M parameters in total) and a BGE-M3 fine-tune (81.0%); at recall@10 its interval overlaps those of its nearest neighbours on both sides. Our four-language model, trained with a capped share of the same Kazakh pairs, is 2.8 points lower at recall@1, with overlapping recall@10 intervals. The Kazakh model also scores higher than the released model on the Uzbek and Kyrgyz versions of Belebele, but our Tajik model, trained without any Turkic pairs, gains as much there, so these gains are not specific to Kazakh training. Our Kazakh Wikipedia test questions come from the same generator family as the training questions, so we rest the main claims on Belebele.

### [74] [daVinci-Prover: Agent-Native Mid-Training for Formal Theorem Proving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16433)
*Wenhong Zhu,Xuefeng Li,Jiashuo Zhang,Yu Chen,Tiantian Mi,Qipeng Guo,Pengfei Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming formal theorem proving. Yet further progress remains constrained by the lack of a transparent and effective data recipe for systematically improving theorem-proving models. In this work, we argue that effective agentic provers require strong mathematical skill priors to ground theorem proving and agentic trajectories to enable long-horizon, interactive proof construction. To this end, we synthesize an agent-native 33.7B-token mid-training corpus covering decomposition, search, self-verification, and revision, together with verifier-grounded agentic trajectories. We further introduce the daVinci-Prover harness, which enables models to construct proofs and interact with a Lean verifier in an isolated workspace, and use it to collect approximately 36K high-quality agent trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. Our mid-training recipe yields an average improvement of 13.7 points over the matched Qwen3-8B SFT-only baseline across MiniF2F, FATE-M, and ProofNet. When applied to the Qwen3.5 series, our approach also yields strong performance across theorem-proving benchmarks and achieves near-saturating MiniF2F performance with memory compaction. The results highlight agent-native mid-training as an effective foundation for developing stronger interactive theorem-proving agents.

### [75] [EvenVLM: A Text and Multimodal Dataset for the Even Language with Vision-Language Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16500)
*Daniil Makovetskii,Ivan Bondarenko*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: We present EvenVLM, the first text and multimodal (VQA) dataset for Even (Lamut), an endangered Northern Tungusic language spoken by approximately 6,800 people in Siberia. Our dataset comprises 50,521 structured Even-Russian entries extracted from dictionary and phrasebook sources via GPT-4o Mini-based parsing, from which we synthetically generate 107,543 training examples spanning translation, grammar, reading comprehension, and semantic classification. To address tokenization inefficiency on Even's agglutinative morphology, we propose a three-step tokenizer expansion algorithm that adds Even-specific graphemes (eng, oe, o-umlaut), whitelisted vocabulary, and BPE merges, reducing average tokens per word by 27% (4.99 to 3.64). Using LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-4B, we adapt the model for text tasks (0.53% trainable parameters, rank 32) and separately for visual question answering (rank 64, frozen vision encoder). Our best configuration achieves 11.4% exact match and a 13.6 weighted score on text benchmarks, 0.1283 chrF for sentence translation, and 65% accuracy on VQA (up from 0% for the base model and text-only fine-tuning). We release our datasets, evaluation benchmarks, and training pipeline to support further research on Even and other low-resource languages.

### [76] [Unibuc - NLP at "Voight-Kampff" Generative AI Detection PAN 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16612)
*Teodor Marchitan,Claudiu Creanga,Liviu P. Dinu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper describes the approach of the Unibuc - NLP team in tackling the "Voight-Kampff" Generative AI Detection task from PAN at CLEF 2025. In the Subtask 1: Voight-Kampff AI Detection Sensitivity we have explored different approaches of leveraging embeddings extracted from LLMs, using either classical ML models or further fine-tuning LLMs with a classification head for the downstream binary classification task. Our experiments showed that using a majority vote ensemble of classical ML models (Light GBM, XGB, Logistic Regression and SVM) is comparable with fine-tuning for downstream task achieving around 99.4% F1 score. For the Subtask 2: Human-AI Collaborative Text Classification we explored a way of combining features at different layers extracted using transformer backbone with layer-wise projection and attentive pooling which proved modest results.

### [77] [Forecasting Sales Delay through Time-aware Analysis of Sales Events in Textual Reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16704)
*Masaya Tsunokake,Yuta Koreeda,Yuhei Niwa,Terufumi Morishita,Teppei Inoue,Hiroaki Ozaki,Yasuhiro Sogawa*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Business-to-business (B2B) companies develop and deliver a one-of-a-kind product in response to a client's orders. To prepare resources for development beforehand, companies estimate dates when they will receive orders from clients in their sales process, called scheduled order dates. However, dates when the companies actually receive orders can differ from the scheduled order dates. This difference increases costs in the development. If the difference could be forecasted before receiving orders, companies could optimize their resource preparation. Towards reducing the costs, we introduce sales delay forecasting, a novel task of forecasting delay days from the scheduled order dates during sales process where sales representatives (sales reps) interact with the clients to receive orders. Sales delay forecasting is challenging because the sales process progress inherently involves uncertainty and depends on the client's willingness to order. To address this task, we propose confidence features which represent sales reps' confidence as a proxy measure of the client's willingness to order. To represent it, our method extracts dates of future sales events anticipated by sales reps from textual reports. To consider whether the confidence objectively looks reasonable, we also introduce status features which describe sales process status based on current date and past events. In experiments using real sales data, our method achieved a 16% lower mean absolute error compared with a feature-based baseline similar to a prior work. Moreover, our method outperformed non-feature-based baselines using large language models, indicating that it is crucial to explicitly create our features.

### [78] [Towards Green Text Generation: Memory-Based Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16714)
*Antal van den Bosch*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Speculative decoding accelerates text generation with large language models by letting a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large verifier checks in a single forward pass. We introduce Olifant, a draft model built on a memory-based classifier. It predicts the next token from a four-token window in under 0.3 ms on CPU, requiring no GPU, no backpropagation, and no accelerator memory. We measure throughput and energy under two verifier regimes on consumer hardware. Without a KV cache, drafting is nearly free: a domain-matched Olifant model reaches 38.1% acceptance on EU legal text, delivering 2.43x throughput and 2.51x lower energy per token than the neural verifier model alone. With a KV-cached verifier, itself a ~10x energy saver, drafting costs matter: a TinyLlama draft model halves throughput and triples energy despite high acceptance, whereas Olifant still yields 1.25x throughput and the lowest energy in the study (93 J per 100 tokens, 14x below the uncached baseline). We further show that KV caching decouples time from energy: verification of longer drafts raises power draw, shifting the energy-optimal draft length below the speed-optimal one. Speculative decoding is not dead in the age of fast verifiers, provided drafting is nearly free.

### [79] [Outcome-Mass Alignment: Controlling Length-Dependent Trajectory Influence in Multi-Turn LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16816)
*Dawei Zhang,Yubin Huangfu,Jessica Fan,Boyu Wei,Likang Wu,Hongke Zhao,Ming He,Zhu Teng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: To keep long interaction contexts tractable, stepwise group-relative training for multi-turn LLM agents materializes each source trajectory into multiple response rows and valid tokens. This expansion creates an outer-accounting problem distinct from within-trajectory credit assignment: row-based outcome statistics can count one episode outcome multiple times, while token-level reduction can assign unequal aggregate objective mass across trajectories. We term these effects outcome-statistics multiplicity and objective-mass imbalance. We introduce Outcome-Mass Alignment (OMA), a two-component method that makes both accounting choices explicit. Outcome Alignment computes outcome statistics over unique source trajectories, while Mass Alignment controls aggregate objective mass after within-trajectory aggregation of optimizer-native token objectives. Neither redesigns the base optimizer's credit assignment, importance ratios, or clipping. Across matched ALFWorld GRPO comparisons at two model scales, where failed trajectories typically expand much more than successful ones, OMA improves matched-horizon endpoint success by 7.0-9.4 percentage points. Ordinary WebShop exhibits weak or reversed expansion-outcome coupling and correspondingly mixed effects, whereas in a success-oriented WebShop setting, WebShop-SOL, OMA improves success nAUC from 0.399 to 0.511. Component ablations and GiGPO and GSPO comparisons further support component separability and cross-optimizer compatibility. These results show that trajectory expansion always defines an implicit weighting rule, but its practical effect depends on how expansion couples to outcomes and optimizer-native updates.

### [80] [Shortcuts or Memorisation? Revisiting Data Corruption in Natural Language Understanding with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16843)
*Aarne Talman,Stergios Chatzikyriakidis*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Pre-trained encoders fine-tuned on natural language inference (NLI) and other language understanding tasks keep much of their accuracy after the input is perturbed, e.g. by removing all nouns or shuffling the words. Does the same hold for large language models (LLMs), and if so, is it because they have seen the benchmarks during pre-training? In this paper we revisit these perturbation experiments with eight LLMs alongside fine-tuned encoders on GLUE and the three rounds of ANLI. Regardless of model size, every system that answers directly retains 36-72% of its above-chance performance without nouns on MNLI compared to only 14-29% on ANLI. Only a model that reasons before answering departs from this pattern. We also check contamination indicators (including exact $n$-gram counts in the public pre-training data of two of the models) and find no link between exposure and robustness. Our strongest evidence comes from 368 new, human-validated items that none of the models can have seen. All eight LLMs keep more of their performance without nouns on items written in MNLI's style than on items written without its cues. When the perturbation instead removes the function words carrying such cues, this advantage reverses. In light of these results, we argue that robustness to perturbation on familiar NLI benchmarks reflects dataset shortcuts rather than memorisation, and tells us more about the benchmark than about the model.

### [81] [Beyond Word Error Rate: A Failure Taxonomy of Streaming Dictation ASR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16919)
*Harras Mansoor,Muhammad Wisal,Hassan Bhatti,Masood Shakir*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Speech recognition (ASR) systems are usually compared by word error rate (WER) on recorded files, after punctuation, capital letters and number format are removed. In dictation, the audio is streamed live and the text goes into the user's message as written, so what matters is which mistakes the user has to fix. The test set, streamed to eleven ASR systems, comprises 106 scripted English dictations from one speaker (read in a quiet room, with a fan on, and whispered), 20 clips in each of eleven other language and dialect sets, and 400 recordings that join clips in two languages. Every error was sorted by a fixed rule into four levels: recognition, output formatting, language handling and, for the self-hosted models, audio dropped before the model. Systems with similar WER failed in different ways. Zoom Scribe and OpenAI's GPT-Live-Transcribe have almost the same WER on quiet English (7.4% and 7.3%), but 34.7% and 8.8% on whispered English. Zoom and both AssemblyAI models left out 26-28% of whispered words, and still 21-26% with their end-of-turn detection relaxed or off; seven other systems left out at most 3%. Qwen3-ASR's 32% came from the speech detection in our own deployment (6% when relaxed). Across 107 EARS speakers, the same four systems lost 7-31% of whispered words, while six others lost under 2%. With only English selected, Gemini, Deepgram and our self-hosted Whisper lost the non-English part of a two-language recording in 86-99% of recordings, against 33-46% with both languages selected, while GPT-Live-Transcribe, OpenAI's realtime Whisper and Meta lost it in at most 20%. Running Whisper behind a Silero voice activity detector that drops audio judged to be silence raised whispered WER from 10.1% to 51.4%. Most English results come from one read speaker. The code, the recordings, both references and every transcript are released.

### [82] [Morphological Simplification in Alzheimer's Disease: Computational Analysis and Identification From Connected Speech](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16968)
*Mohamed Zakaria Kurdi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Purpose: Morphology is often regarded as relatively spared in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and is rarely modeled in connected speech. This study asked which morphological features distinguish speakers with AD from healthy controls, how well morphology classifies AD compared with other linguistic levels and BERT-based models, and whether the signal exceeds transcript length and vocabulary. Method: Fifty-five automatic measures in eight families, seven of them new and theory-motivated, were computed from participant speech in the ADReSS Cookie Theft descriptions (78 AD, 78 controls) and analyzed with group comparisons, equivalence tests, SHAP, family ablation, likelihood-ratio tests, feature-selection classifiers, and BERT-based models. The automatic measures were validated manually, and models were transferred to two other corpora. Results: Nineteen of 38 measures differed between groups: speakers with AD produced fewer suffixed and inflected words, shorter verbs and nouns, and fewer present-progressive but more past-tense forms (largest effect r = -0.42), whereas errors were rare and statistically equivalent between groups. Eight measures survived adjustment for length and lexical frequency. With test-set feature selection, morphology reached a macro-F1 of 0.85, on par with syntax and above fine-tuned BERT (0.80 over five seeds); fully cross-validated selection gave 0.62. Adding morphology to BERT improved AUC (0.91 vs. 0.89) but not macro-F1. Transfer was limited, although two thirds of the effects kept their direction in mild cognitive impairment. Conclusions: AD connected speech shows morphological simplification and temporal reanchoring rather than breakdown. Morphology is more informative than its reputation suggests. Keywords: Alzheimer's disease; morphology; connected speech; ADReSS; inflection; tense and aspect; SHAP; machine learning; BERT

### [83] [Similar but Not Redundant: Embedding-Gated Refinement for High-Granularity Topic Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17030)
*Daniel Denley,Robert L. Nicol,Mike J. Chantler*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: High-granularity topic modelling extracts hundreds of niche topics from a corpus, yet this regime is rarely studied and is more commonly framed as a failure mode: "over-clustering," in which coherent themes fragment into redundant subtopics. We argue that this framing conflates genuine redundancy with topics that are semantically similar but meaningfully distinct, and that the central challenge in high-granularity modelling is separating the two. Recent post-hoc refinement methods address topic redundancy through either embedding-based similarity thresholding or LLM-guided merging. We show that neither suffices in high-granularity settings and propose embedding-gated iterative merge (EGIM), a hybrid approach that iteratively generates context-rich topic representations, uses embedding similarity to propose candidate merges across the topic space, then applies LLM judgement to accept only genuinely redundant pairs while preserving niche distinctions. Across two patent corpora and one legal corpus, LLM judgement rejects 83% of embedding-identified candidates as non-redundant. EGIM improves discriminability on merged topics by 25-55% over a prior iterative LLM baseline while better preserving the original topic distribution.

### [84] [Optimal Single-History Tokenization Disambiguation for Provably Secure Linguistic Steganography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17091)
*Feng Jiang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Provably secure linguistic steganography assumes that the receiver recovers the sender's tokens, but a text channel delivers only text, and ambiguous tokenizations break extraction. Existing fixes change the distribution, synchronize whole pools of tokens at a capacity that collapses with large vocabularies, or track several token histories. We prove that if extraction is exact and error-free across full-support language models, a single-history receiver is confined to a prefix-free candidate set at every step -- even if it reads the entire future text and the sender constrains later steps -- and must therefore give up the stop entropy, the entropy of deciding whether each prefix token ends there. Fixing these stop decisions on the prefix forest with shared randomness yields coin projection: a closed-form scheme that attains the bound, works with any distribution coder in one model call per token, preserves ordinary sampling, and refines SyncPool for every key. Across English, Chinese and Japanese, ambiguous text is rare (at most 11 in 1,000 tokens), yet the stop entropy at word and morpheme prefixes takes 7.2-9.0% of the entropy at every step; SyncPool's further loss comes from space and single-byte UTF-8 hubs that merge subtrees while carrying almost no stop uncertainty. Coin projection keeps 91-93% of the string entropy for the coder at every vocabulary size; with the full vocabulary, it turns 2.16-6.85 times as much entropy into message bits as SyncPool and recovers every completed message.

### [85] [Disentangling Spurious Correlations: How IRM Handles Diverse Shortcuts in Text Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17107)
*Paul Grunenwald,Benoît Crabbé,Guillaume Wisniewski,Pirmin Lemberger*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: In NLP, models trained via Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) often exploit spurious correlations, such as dialectal markers, at the expense of robust linguistic features, thereby degrading their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) aims to suppress such shortcuts by identifying predictive relationships that remain stable across environments, but its practical utility for NLP remains debated. We use a causality-driven framework to evaluate IRM under three shortcut-generating mechanisms: label-generated features, confounding, and selection bias. Our results show that IRM successfully rejects shortcuts across the evaluated causal and anti-causal structures, including under limited environmental variation and increasing label noise. We then extend our analysis beyond controlled synthetic artifacts to two less constrained settings: gender-profession associations in Bias in Bios and semantically loaded actor-name shortcuts in ActorCorr. These experiments show that invariant learning can mitigate more realistic textual shortcuts, while semantically meaningful features require careful calibration of the invariance penalty.

### [86] [Learning When Diffusion Language Models Should Regenerate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17320)
*Minhae Oh,Jeonghye Kim,Jinwoo Koo,Yeongoon Kim,Jimin Seo,Minsik Seol,Jungwoo Lee*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Remasking allows diffusion language models to revisit generated text, but effective correction requires knowing when and what to revise. Our diagnosis on Sudoku reveals two gaps. Hidden states contain error information that token confidence does not reliably expose, and remasking an isolated error usually reproduces it when the surrounding context remains fixed. These findings motivate DiVR , a verifier that predicts whether a partially generated sequence will reach a correct answer. Trained on the final correctness of the model's own trajectories, DiVR decides when to regenerate a block and which alternative to retain, while the generator itself stays unchanged. On five reasoning benchmarks with LLaDA-8B-Base, DiVR raises the average accuracy of the fine-tuned generator from 35.3\% to 43.4\% at $1.9$-$3.5\times$ the cost of greedy decoding, above search baselines that use $3.8$-$7.4\times$. It also complements post-training such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and generalizes to other generators, including Dream.

### [87] [RMIT-ADM+S at TREC RAG 2026: Research Agents, Retriever Ablations, and Open-Weight Replication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16425)
*Oleg Zendel,Kun Ran,Chenglong Ma,Nguyen Khoi Vo,Shuai Wang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: 本文系统报告了 RMIT-ADM+S 团队参加 TREC 2026 RAG 赛道（ClimbMix 语料）的结果：提交 7 个基于"研究代理"（research agent）的系统，涵盖专有模型（GPT-5.6-Sol/Luna）与开放权重模型（GLM-5、GPT-OSS-120B、Qwen3-Next-80B），并在检索器、写作模型与代理编排三个维度上做了消融。核心结论是：写作模型选择与相邻分块扩展是影响答案质量的最主要因素；官方 NIST 评测中 7 个系统有 6 个在三类 rubric/nugget 集合上均超过赛道中位数，最佳系统 brief-hybrid 在 B1 vital 覆盖率上并列赛道最高（0.892）；同时发现自动化覆盖率指标与人类偏好排序存在系统性分歧——开放权重 owa-glm5 以 $0.524/题的成本在 B1 人类对比中显著优于 $2.823/题的 sol-research-first。


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 研究动机包含三点：其一，检验开放权重（open-weight）研究代理能否在更低成本下达到与专有闭源模型相当的质量，并解释性能差距的来源（RQ1）；其二，系统比较模型、检索与编排选择对答案质量与 token/金钱成本的影响（RQ2）；其三，考察多阶段编排是否真能优于简单的单循环代理，或只能部分弥补较弱写作模型的能力（RQ3）。作者延续此前在 LiveRAG（生成辅助检索与重排）与 MMU-RAG（轻量开放权重模型的自适应检索）上的竞赛系统研究，并指出 LLM-as-judge 评估对裁判模型与呈现顺序高度敏感这一方法论问题，主张使用互补的评估信号。

Method: 方法为系统化的"设计因子分解 + 单因子爬坡消融 + 官方评测"三段式。检索侧：将 ClimbMix-400B-shuffle（6,543 分片、约 5.63 亿文档）做段落感知分块（目标 200–500 token，硬上限 700，1.3 token/词），构建含 921,892,634 分块的 BM25 索引（Lucene/Anserini，k1=0.9、b=0.4），稠密检索用自微调 jina-v5-nano（256 维）配合 DiskANN（MIP，R=64、Lbuild=100、32 字节 PQ）；混合检索用无权 RRF（κ=60）；facetrag 额外支持 Boolean 与 Cottentail 的最短子串排序（SSR）。检索器微调采用"分阶段证据 + commit_context"机制导出代理轨迹标签（2,143 条检索行、4,857 正样本与 12,889 负样本），在 95 主题/1,587 子查询上以 Tevatron+InfoNCE（τ=0.05、batch 64、4 epoch、LoRA r=16）训练，24 个留出主题 nDCG@10 从 0.751 提升到 0.793。系统侧：七个运行——sol-default（单对话 100 轮）、sol-research-first（计划+盲义务侦察+40 轮循环）、brief-base/brief-hybrid（前置需求简报+单次评审）、owa-glm5（GLM-5 全流程+盲侦察）、facets（GPT-5.6-Luna 分面分解）、facetrag（GPT-OSS-120B 编排器+Qwen3-Next-80B 分析器，MMR 式策展）。评估侧：预提交用 RAGDoll 做逐点评分（约 31 条准则、六维度+总体 0–3）与双向呈现的 pairwise arena（30/119 主题）；官方用 vital_strict/all_strict 覆盖率、Tukey HSD 显著性、Bradley–Terry 人类对比评分（分批拟合）、符号翻转检验、Flesch–Kincaid 可读性测量与 Spearman 相关分析。

Result: 预提交消融显示写作模型影响最大：相对 GPT-5.6-Sol 基线（2.267/3），Terra/Luna 下降 0.40、Qwen3-Next 下降 0.867、GPT-OSS 下降 1.067；12 项结构改动中 10 项影响 ≤0.067；禁用 ±1 相邻分块扩展在 Sol 下降 0.067、Qwen3 下降 0.133；Hybrid RRF 使逐点评分升至 2.333 且在 119 主题上搜索数减 14.4%、处理 token 减 8.2%、估算生成成本降 8.5%（$2.156 vs $2.356）。编辑器敏感性极强：同一 20 主题、仅更换裁判模型，胜率由 17.5%（Sol）变为 45.0%（Luna）、25.0%（Terra），且存在明显位置偏置。官方 NIST 评测中 7 系统有 6 个在三个集合上均超中位数；brief-hybrid 的 all_strict 在三批次均为最高（0.909/0.723/0.565），并与 sol-research-first 并列 B1 vital 全赛道最高 0.892，但四个领先专有系统在六项覆盖指标上 Tukey HSD 均无显著差异。facetrag 最弱（B1 vital 0.600）。人类对比出现方向性分歧：Batch 1 强烈偏好开放权重 owa-glm5（BT 1212.8 vs 1062.7；13/17 主题占优，符号翻转 p=0.006），尽管其覆盖率更低；Batch 2 反向，sol-research-first 领先（1124.7 vs 1049.0）但主题级不显著（p=0.110）。owa-glm5 平均 Flesch–Kincaid 15.7 对 22.2（17/17 主题更易读，p<0.001），但可读性差异与偏好差距无显著关联（ρ=+0.27, p=0.30），仅能视为可能因素。内部 arena 与官方覆盖率排序仅中等一致（Kendall τ=0.33–0.60）。诊断还发现一个"评审环节失效"案例：owa-glm5 在 topic 65 上评审阶段只返回了 21 词的修正句而非完整修订，导致 0/0 覆盖率。

Conclusion: 结论为三点：RQ1——开放权重代理在部分指标上有竞争力（超过赛道中位数、成本仅 $0.524/题）但未能在覆盖率上稳定匹敌领先专有系统，且存在综合与修订环节弱点（Batch 2 nugget 覆盖明显落后，评审失败实例）；RQ2——写作模型选择是影响最大的因素，相邻分块扩展的收益随写作模型而变，Hybrid RRF 带来最明确的效率提升且在官方 B1 vital 上并列第一；RQ3——复杂编排并无一致优势，sol-research-first 比 sol-default 多耗 81% token 却几乎没有 Batch 2 覆盖增益，facetrag 的多阶段高检索量反而最弱，且因模型/检索/提示同时变化，编排效应未被单独隔离。总体论断是：agentic RAG 不存在唯一最优设计，各系统在覆盖率、人类偏好、鲁棒性与效率间各有取舍；评估协议的选择本身同样具有实质性影响，内部自动评测、官方 nugget/rubric 覆盖率与人类对比可能给出不同排序，因此系统选型应同时选择能反映目标使用场景的评估方法，并结合互补信号而非依赖单一指标。

Abstract: We describe the RMIT-ADM+S team's participation in the TREC 2026 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) track using the ClimbMix corpus. We submitted seven research-agent runs using proprietary OpenAI and open-weight models, exploring different retrieval strategies, writer models, and agent workflows. Pre-submission ablations identified writer selection and adjacent-chunk expansion as the main factors affecting answer quality. In the official NIST evaluation, six of seven runs exceeded the track median across all three rubric/nugget collections. Our best-performing run, brief-hybrid, achieved the highest all-item coverage among our submissions and tied the track maximum (0.892) for Batch-1 vital coverage. Human side-by-side preferences differed across evaluation batches: the open-weight owa-glm5 led Batch 1 despite lower automated coverage, while sol-research-first led Batch 2. These findings highlight differences between automated coverage measures and human preferences, as well as the potential of lower-cost open-weight models for research-agent systems.

</details>


### [88] [Sheaf-Inspired Structured Scoring Extensions of LightGCN for Collaborative Filtering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17226)
*Ksenia Belkovskaya,Timur Lidzhiev,Maria Stebliy,Alexander Tarakanov*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Graph-based collaborative filtering learns user and item representations by propagating embeddings over a user--item interaction graph. We investigate a modular, sheaf-inspired scoring extension placed on top of a three-layer LightGCN backbone. The motivation comes from cellular sheaves, where local vector spaces are related by linear restriction maps; here, this idea motivates structured, pair-dependent transformations of user and item embeddings rather than a change to graph propagation. We compare the identity inner-product scorer, diagonal, rank-one low-rank, and full matrix residual scorers, and a parameter-matched residual MLP baseline (\texttt{mlp\_full}) on Amazon-Book, Gowalla, MovieLens-1M, and Yelp2018. We report ranking quality and catalog coverage at cutoffs 10 and 20. The selected structured variants show modest, dataset-dependent changes in ranking quality and sometimes substantial changes in coverage. Our method is inspired by sheaf geometry but does not construct a cellular sheaf or implement sheaf-Laplacian diffusion; the experiments therefore do not establish a causal benefit from sheaf geometry itself.

### [89] [Measuring, Revealing and Mitigating Harmful Content Propagation in Recommender Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15160)
*Xiaokun Zhang,Youlin Wu,Junyu Lu,Jiamin Chen,Zhaochun Ren,Hongfei Lin,Fenglong Ma,Xue Liu,Chen Ma*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Recommender systems help users navigate vast amounts of information by filtering content according to their historical behaviors. As these systems increasingly shape everyday information access, they largely determine the content users are exposed to. However, current research typically prioritizes catering to user interest, while overlooking the existence and propagation of harmful content, such as violence, hate speech, and pornography. In this work, we take a systematic step toward investigating harmful content in recommender systems from three aspects: measuring, revealing, and mitigating. First, we construct datasets with harmfulness-related annotations and present new evaluation metrics to quantitatively measure the harmfulness of recommendation results. Second, our empirical analysis reveals that users tend to engage with harmful content and prevailing recommendation methods often contribute to the proliferation of such content. Third, to address this issue, we introduce a generic framework, MitiHarm, which integrates harmfulness-related signals into both item and user representation learning. Experiments show that MitiHarm can significantly mitigate the propagation of harmful content while preserving user satisfaction. Resources of this work are available at this https URL .

### [90] [When Direction Matters: Diagnosing Relational Instruction Following in Dense Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15417)
*Zhanyu Wu,Richong Zhang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Dense retrievers increasingly claim the ability to condition retrieval on natural-language relevance criteria beyond a short query. We identify a specific weakness in this capability: the evaluated models perform well when lexical or attribute cues distinguish the target, but become much less reliable when relevance depends on a directional relation over the same entities. We introduce SwitchIR, a controlled diagnostic that contrasts Constraint Shift and Explicit Filtering with Relational Flip, where the query and document pair remain fixed while the requested relation direction reverses. Across representative embedding and late-interaction retrievers, the primary joint metric is high on the two cue-available controls and consistently low on Relational Flip; the same ordering persists in an LLM-assisted, manually reviewed realistic variant. An exact margin decomposition shows that both directions are correct only when the direction-sensitive query--document interaction exceeds the direction-invariant pair preference. Empirically, direction-sensitive changes are common, but their aligned interaction is usually too weak to overcome that preference. Diagnostic fine-tuning shows that models can learn relational behavior that generalizes across relation families, with stronger generalization in the larger model.

### [91] [SurvEval: Listwise Re-Ranking Evaluator via Survival-Based Exposure and Multi-Objective Value Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15434)
*YaChen Yan,Liubo Li*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Re-ranking is a crucial stage in recommender systems, yet existing evaluators oversimplify user browsing assumptions and collapse multi-objective signals into a single scalar, limiting their ability to reflect true listwise utility. We propose \textbf{SurvEval}, a listwise evaluator that jointly models user exposure and item value for re-ranking evaluation. We formalize the sequential browsing process as a discrete-time survival model, deriving monotonically decreasing reaching probabilities that capture the cascading structure of user browsing. We further introduce a multi-objective value estimation module with dedicated per-objective prediction heads and uncertainty-based loss weighting to adaptively balance objectives of varying scales and noise levels. Both components are jointly optimized via a unified transformer backbone, and the listwise utility is obtained by summing the position-wise products of reaching probabilities and conditional item value estimates. Extensive experiments on KuaiRand and Avito demonstrate that SurvEval achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art baselines.

### [92] [ReAlign: Reward-Guided Preference Alignment for Generative Re-Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15445)
*YaChen Yan,Liubo Li*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Re-ranking refines the upstream ranked list to maximize listwise user utility. Existing two-stage generator-evaluator methods decouple list generation from list evaluation, leaving the generator without direct access to the listwise utility signal, while scoring-based one-stage methods score items under a fixed upstream permutation context without explicitly searching the permutation space. We propose \textbf{ReAlign}, a reward-guided preference alignment framework that couples a listwise reward model with a candidate-aware autoregressive generator. The reward model decomposes the listwise reward into position-wise contributions, modeling user exposure through a survival-based exposure module and item value through per-objective heads for heterogeneous engagement signals. The generator is trained in two stages: supervised pre-training on logged exposure lists to establish a relevance prior, followed by reward-guided post-training that aligns the generator with the reward model through complementary distribution and ranking alignment over within-pool standardized rewards. Extensive offline experiments show that ReAlign consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines.

### [93] [Bag of concepts can enhance other text representations for medical systematic review screening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15798)
*Radosław Pytlak,Paweł Cichosz,Bartłomiej Fajdek,Bogdan Jastrzębski*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: The paper examines the choice of text representation for semi-automated systematic literature review (SLR) systems based on active learning. Motivated by the insufficient attention that the bag of concepts representation has received so far, the paper discusses the implementation and experimental evaluation of several variations thereof. The experimental study was performed on medical SLR case studies, with results reported for random forest classification, cluster initialization and uncertainty sampling. The utility of bag of concepts features obtained using different ontologies is evaluated by applying them within the active learning framework to sequentially create classification models based on training data iteratively expanded with expert annotations. Systematic experiments compare BoW, BoC, PubMedBERT, Jina, Gemma and Qwen3 representations, together with combinations of BoC and each of the other representations. The evaluation uses workload savings and performance profiles adapted from optimization benchmarking. The results suggest that concept-based features can provide complementary information, with the BoC-augmented representations achieving higher mean workload savings on the DERP cases than their corresponding base representations. The Qwen3+BoC representation gives the best average performance in this comparison. The effects of augmentation vary across case studies and base representations. The paper also concentrates on the impact of ontology choice on document classification outcomes. In particular, the paper compares the predictive value of bag of concepts representations based on chosen ontologies with that of representations obtained using MedCAT with a UMLS-based dictionary.

### [94] [From Tokens to Behaviors: Rethinking Generative Recommendation for User Trajectory Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16159)
*Jiaqi Wang,Hanchen Yang,Hengyu Zhang,Hongxu Ma,Wenqi Rao,Hongyang Wang,Zhongbo Sun,Renliang Qian,Weixin Chen,Wengen Li,Jihong Guan,Shuigeng Zhou,Qingpeng Cai,Peng Jiang,Hong Cheng*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: User behavior trajectory prediction (UBTP) aims to capture how a user's needs evolve over time by predicting the sequence of future interactions from that user's interaction history. Recent generative recommendation (GR) methods address this task through autoregressive generation of semantic IDs (SIDs). However, serial SID decoding couples token generation with behavior state transitions and requires multiple dependent steps per interaction. Discrete item feedback overlooks predictive uncertainty, and teacher-forced training leaves a training-inference gap in trajectory generation. To address these limitations, we propose TraGR, a behavior-aware generative recommendation framework that aligns generation, feedback, and learning with successive user behaviors. Its behavior-level architecture predicts SID tokens in parallel within each interaction and models behavioral transitions through recurrent state updates, with joint SID and item-level supervision. Probability feedback combines the selected behavior with a probability-weighted summary of alternatives to guide subsequent predictions. Relation-aware trajectory learning incorporates collaborative transition signals and later credit assignment into training on model-generated trajectories. Experiments on four public datasets demonstrate that TraGR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across different prediction horizons. Code: this https URL .

### [95] [GA-HEL: A Knowledge-Driven Expert System for Open-Set, Granularity-Aware Hierarchical Event Linking in Social Media](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16194)
*Shengqi Zhou,Zhigang Liu,Wenxiang Zhu,Zhentao Cang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Social-media event intelligence requires a system to determine whether a post belongs to a registered event space, identify the supported hierarchy path, and stop at the deepest level warranted by the evidence. We formulate this requirement as open-set hierarchical event linking over frozen Storyline--Episode--Atomic Event Cards. GA-HEL implements a three-stage, knowledge-driven expert-system funnel: open-set scope control limits candidate exposure before hierarchical reasoning, hierarchy-aware decoders select a supported path and depth, and deterministic legal-path validation checks each record before database-compatible use. A 200-post Pilot supports task and mechanism development, while a separately annotated 497-post Expansion set evaluates transfer across four held-out Storylines and a hard-negative pool. Method implementations, prompts, Event Cards, candidate order, and six systems' predictions were frozen before Expansion Gold annotation. The resulting evaluation combines end-to-end hierarchical matching, open-set rejection, structural validation, ablation, cross-Storyline analysis, and an independent expert reannotation of a fixed audited subset. GA-HEL remains competitive with strong global full-card reasoning while providing explicit scope control and hierarchy-valid structured records. Error analysis identifies unsupported descent from Episode-level evidence to Atomic Events as the dominant remaining challenge. The task definition, frozen resource, and auditable protocol provide a reproducible foundation for scope-aware event intelligence. Code, Event Cards, labels, frozen predictions, and evaluation scripts are available at this https URL .

### [96] [CURATOR: Scalable Fine-grained Evidence Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16366)
*Shib Dasgupta,Bandish Parikh,Rashmi Gangadharaiah*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides entire retrieved passages to the LLM, even though only a handful of spans within them contain the evidence pertaining to the question. While precise selection of these spans can improve context utilization, identifying them in isolation is challenging. A span may appear irrelevant by itself, and deciding whether to retain it may require examining other retrieved information. One can evaluate each span's candidacy with the full retrieved context, but this is computationally inefficient as the same text must be processed repeatedly. Pretrained decision model can be used to efficiently evaluate multiple spans simultaneously, allowing each decision to consider the surrounding spans as well. However, our experiments show that their ability to identify relevant evidence deteriorates as the number of simultaneous decisions increases. To address this, we introduce CURATOR, a fine-tuned decision model trained to make reliable evidence-selection decisions over large candidate sets. By training a decision model to select varying numbers of supporting spans from large candidate pools, CURATOR develops the capability to select evidence for RAG while retaining the computational efficiency of joint decision-making. We observe that CURATOR maintains a strong evidence discrimination capability as the number of candidates increases, generalizes across different tasks and document domains, and improves downstream RAG performance, particularly when the available context is limited.

### [97] [TriGen: A Generative Paradigm for Trigger-Induced Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16395)
*Muyu Zou,Haibo Xing,Shunye Tang,Liyan Tie,Lingyu Mu,Yandong Wang,Jinxin Hu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Generative recommendation typically operates under the User-Induced Recommendation (UIR) setting, predicting target items by autoregressively generating semantic IDs as a passive continuation of long-term user history. However, this paradigm overlooks Trigger-Induced Recommendation (TIR), an essential industrial scenario where a user click triggers an immediate follow-up feed. In TIR, recommendations must dynamically align with the instant trigger intent without compromising historical preference continuity. Traditional TIR methods rely on discriminative scoring and cannot guide token-level generation, while existing generative models lack mechanisms to reconcile this structural tension. To address this challenge, we propose TriGen, establishing a tailored generative paradigm for trigger-induced recommendation. TriGen introduces calibrated tail injection to re-encode local history, adaptively arbitrates between persistent tastes and immediate impulses via dynamic gating, and applies position-specific transformations to sustain level-aware trigger guidance across decoding steps. Extensive offline evaluations confirm consistent gains over competitive baselines. Furthermore, online A/B tests across six country markets demonstrate significant revenue and GMV improvements, leading to the full production deployment of TriGen.

### [98] [ReSID: Rethinking Long-Tail Retrieval in Generative Recommendation through Item Reachability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16404)
*Muyu Zou,Shunye Tang,Yi Xu,Haibo Xing,Yandong Wang,Lingyu Mu,Jinxin Hu*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Generative recommendation (GR) represents items with discrete Semantic IDs (SIDs) and casts retrieval as sequence generation. Under skewed interaction distributions and tight serving budgets, GR struggles to retrieve long-tail items. In this work, we are the first to study long-tail reachability across the complete pipeline of SID construction, decoding, and matching. We find that under equal code lengths, parallel SID construction consistently outperforms sequential SIDs on tail items. Moreover, even when full generation fails, decoded sequences carry locally consistent information that retrieves relevant tail items via partial matching. Yet this recovery is bounded by upstream search, failing once beam search prunes all prefixes completable within a fixed mismatch tolerance. Motivated by these findings, we propose ReSID to jointly preserve and recover tail candidates. Built on long parallel SIDs, ReSID pairs popularity-debiased and user-semantic-aware beam search to keep promising paths alive with partial SID matching to recover items from surviving tokens. ReSID achieves state-of-the-art long-tail retrieval while maintaining competitive overall accuracy, with lower latency and higher throughput under narrow beams. ReSID is deployed in our production system, serving main user traffic with substantial business gains. We release our complete code and model checkpoints to support full reproducibility and real-world deployment at this https URL .

### [99] [AntEmbed: Dual-Mode Multimodal Embedding Model for Efficient and Fine-Grained Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16405)
*Kehang Jia,Teng Liu,Juntao Li,Hua Chen,Jinxiong Chang,Xiaobo Liang,Min Zhang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Discriminative embeddings encode original multimodal inputs efficiently but struggle with fine-grained semantics. Generative embeddings use reasoning to capture query intent and relevance evidence, but incur higher computational costs. We propose AntEmbed, a dual-mode multimodal embedding model that supports efficient retrieval and reasoning-enhanced fine-grained matching in a unified embedding space. First, we construct retrieval-oriented reasoning content that captures query intent and confusion-aware semantic evidence. We treat original and reasoning-enhanced candidate inputs as semantically equivalent views, and use multi-positive contrastive learning with a single embedding token to align discriminative and generative embeddings. Second, cross-mode self-distillation transfers fine-grained semantic information from reasoning-enhanced to original representations through candidate similarity-distribution distillation and query representation alignment. This strengthens discriminative embeddings without requiring additional online reasoning. Both retrieval modes share a single candidate index. On MMEB-v2, AntEmbed-8B achieves an overall score of 81.5 with reasoning-enhanced embeddings, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.1 points.

### [100] [Active Learning of Approximate LLM Ranking for Energy-Efficient Retrieval of Long Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16488)
*Ohad Porat,Elad Yom-Tov*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Search engines and Large Language Models (LLMs) offer complementary strengths for document retrieval: lexical retrievers which rely on keyword matching are fast and energy-efficient, whereas LLMs capture semantic meaning and excel at interpreting long, context-rich queries. However, this comes at a cost that is computationally and energetically prohibitive. We propose the LLM Active Approximation Model (LAAM), a hybrid retrieval framework that introduces a lightweight learned predictor which serves as an intermediary between semantic retrieval and LLM retrieval. LAAM is refined through an active learning loop where an LLM labels a small number of documents. By concentrating LLM evaluations on the most informative documents, the framework substantially reduces inference cost while preserving retrieval effectiveness. We evaluate the proposed framework on TREC Robust 2004 using Lucene with BM25 retrieval and DeepSeek v3 as the LLM, under three levels of query verbosity. For verbose queries, LAAM achieves 87% of average P@10 achieved by DeepSeek's reranking (0.459 vs. 0.526), while requiring only 3.3% of the per-query energy consumption. LAAM is statistically significantly better than BM25 and is indistinguishable from DeepSeek on average precision, though not on MAP (Friedman test, P<0.05 with post-hoc testing). Overall, our results demonstrate that selectively approximating LLM relevance judgments through active learning enables retrieval accuracy to be controlled directly through the evaluation (and consequently energy) budget. Rather than committing to either inexpensive (and less accurate) lexical retrieval or exhaustive (and expensive) LLM reranking, our framework exposes a continuous spectrum of operating points along the energy--accuracy curve, allowing practitioners to select how to trade retrieval quality with computational budget.

### [101] [KuaiRecV2: Benchmarking Large-Scale Continual Learning for Diversified and Multi-task Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16795)
*Chenxu Li,Shuchang Liu,Hantao Shu,Wei Yuan,Zhe Xu,Guoqing Hu,Yan Wang,Biao Yang,Xiang Li,Cheng Ling,Fan Yang,Yongqi Liu,Lantao Hu,Han Li,Kaiqiao Zhan,Kun Gai,An Zhang,Xiang Wang*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Recommender systems, which retrieve items of interest to users based on their interaction histories, have recently witnessed several key technological advancements, benefiting from the semantic representation space and model-data scaling. Nevertheless, practitioners and researchers have frequently encountered critical inconsistencies between simple offline evaluations and complex online results, and this gap still exists in the era of large models. In this work, we address several key factors that contribute to this inconsistency: 1) the \textit{large-scale continual learning challenge} that assumes a practical demand to maintain long-term model effectiveness under dynamic item pools and distributional shifts; 2) the \textit{combinatorial diversity challenge} that requires the generation strategy to solve the accuracy-diversity trade-off in both the finer token level and the holistic item level; and 3) the \textit{multi-task reward balancing challenge}, which is particularly critical for modern generative models that can accurately model the sequence distribution but are less controllable for the multi-task demands. To address these challenges and further pave the way for the development of more realistic recommendation solutions, we introduce KuaiRecV2, a deliberately constructed benchmark with industrial-level datasets from Kuaishou. Specifically, we provide a large-scale interaction dataset with million-scale multi-modal item information and long-term interaction records across 30 days, with a dynamic video candidate pool. Additionally, we provide a rigorous benchmark that evaluates retrieval accuracy, diversity, and multi-task performance in one rubric system, where an effective advancement occurs if and only if the new method improves all metrics. The code is available at this https URL

### [102] [SignalAudit-QD: A Reproducible Audit Resource for External Signals in AI-Query Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16947)
*Amir Rafe,Iman Jamshidi,Gourab Sil,Subasish Das*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: SignalAudit-QD is a reproducible audit resource for testing whether a dated public signal adds information beyond query history in a fixed 20-term U.S. AI panel. It aligns two archived Google Trends extractions with eight USPTO AI-patent publication streams and releases origin-indexed predictions, paired losses, provenance, executable tests, and tamper-evident run manifests. Both inputs are retrospective reconstructions obtained after the modeled 2020--2023 origins; the task is therefore a pseudo-origin assay within frozen measurement vintages, not a historical deployment simulation. In the designated one-month comparison, adding a two-component patent block to a level ridge changes macro mean absolute error by +0.0012 Trends points, with conditional 95% moving-block interval [-0.0363,+0.0387]. This establishes neither aggregate benefit nor equivalence. Alternative dimensions, semantic mapping, patent definitions, a second extraction, and a three-month horizon remain unresolved; persistence-anchored and nonlinear hosts instead show model-specific worsening, tiny for the anchored fit. Matched timing controls expose availability assumptions, while a planted-signal assay detects only the largest tested injection. A within-query high-interest alert demonstrates the released interface but not online utility. The contribution is a bounded negative case study and an extensible evidence schema for auditing external-signal claims in temporal information retrieval.

### [103] [Evaluation of Music Version Retrieval Methods for Setlist Identification in Live Concerts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17070)
*Andres Ferraro,Albin Correya*

Main category: cs.IR

TL;DR: Automatic setlist identification aims to identify the songs performed in live concert recordings by matching noisy and variable-quality audio against a database of reference tracks. This task presents challenges beyond conventional music version identification, including substantial arrangement differences, background noise, and the need to process continuous recordings efficiently at large scale. In this work, we evaluate modern music version retrieval methods for setlist identification using the ASID benchmark, comparing the established Re-MOVE system with CLEWS and NAVE, an internal neural audio version embedding model. Our results show that NAVE and CLEWS substantially outperform Re-MOVE. Notably, NAVE uses 256-dimensional embeddings, compared with 1024 dimensions for CLEWS, providing a four-fold reduction in embedding storage while achieving better retrieval performance. We further evaluate music/non-music gating and find modest improvements in detection and temporal coverage, while qualitative analysis suggests that such preprocessing can improve recognition boundaries beyond what the standard ASID metrics capture. Overall, the results demonstrate that segment-level audio embeddings provide a strong basis for scalable setlist identification and that compact representations can achieve strong accuracy under realistic live-concert conditions at much lower storage and serving cost.
