### [382] [Sparse Matrix Multiplication Exponent 1.5 in the Low-bandwidth Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15201)
*Chetan Gupta,Jukka Suomela,Hossein Vahidi*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: We study sparse matrix multiplication in the low-bandwidth model: $n$ computers multiply two $n\times n$ matrices, and each computer can send and receive one $O(\log n)$-bit message per round. The input matrices are uniformly sparse, meaning that there are at most $d$ nonzero entries in each row and column, and the task is to compute a uniformly sparse part of their product. In prior work, Gupta et al.~(SPAA 2022) presented an $O(d^{1.907})$-round algorithm over fields for this problem when the sparsity structure is globally known in advance (this is referred to as the supported setting). The upper bound was later improved to $O(d^{1.832})$ rounds. In this work, we give a deterministic algorithm that solves this problem in $O(d^{3/2})$ rounds in the supported setting, improving the previous bounds over fields and semirings.

### [383] [MoE Pretraining:Parallelism Layout Changes the Model, Not Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15271)
*Esther Xin*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are trained across many machines, and the way the work is split, the parallelism layout, often changes between runs: a job resumes on a different GPU count, a cluster is resized, or an ablation runs on a new setup. In exact arithmetic the layout should not matter, but in real arithmetic it changes the order in which numbers are added, and some MoE rules such as load balancing and expert capacity are often computed per machine. We ask whether the layout changes the trained MoE model. We pretrain the same small MoE language models (25M to 117M parameters, 20M FineWeb-Edu tokens) with the same seed, data and hyperparameters under 9 data-parallel and expert-parallel layouts, in fp32 on CPUs and fp16 on a GPU, and compare each run with the effect of a new random seed. Across 80 runs we find: (1) The layout does not change model quality, but it does change the model: final predictions differ about 80% as much as with a new seed, and over 90% of routing decisions differ. Any layout, a one-bit change to one weight, or a different CPU thread count has the same effect. (2) The cause is the router: decisions that flip are almost exactly those where two experts were nearly tied (AUC 0.97 to 1.00 in the first 16 steps). (3) More, smaller experts create more near-ties (2.7% with 8 experts, 23% with 64) and less reproducible routing (68% vs. 100% of decisions differ), but outputs do not drift further. (4) A dense model of the same active size is far more stable (0.12x the seed level in fp32, 0.58x in fp16), while the MoE reaches about 0.8x at both precisions and twice as fast. (5) When pretraining resumes on a new layout, timing matters: switching at 84% of pretraining barely changes the final model, while switching at 10%, just after warm-up, changes it substantially. We release code, run logs and data.

### [384] [SoK: Design Choices in Tendermint BFT Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15847)
*Sanaz Taheri-Boshrooyeh,Yahya Hassanzadeh-Nazarabadi*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Tendermint is a consensus protocol that tolerates Byzantine faults, implemented first by the Tendermint Core engine and now by CometBFT. Realizing the protocol's separation of agreement from execution, the Application Blockchain Interface (ABCI) of these engines keeps consensus apart from the replicated application, so one engine can serve many independent proof-of-stake chains. A sustained body of research proposes changes that span the protocol's mechanisms, from vote dissemination to block proposal and reward distribution, yet to our knowledge no survey studies the protocol and these works as one family, and broader surveys do not take Tendermint as their subject. We describe the baseline, the protocol as consolidated from its original descriptions, by its design choices. Each is a decision, such as how votes spread or how proposers rotate, through which the baseline provides safety and liveness or another property under its fault and timing model. We classify each work by the design choice it renegotiates, that is, modifies or replaces, by the properties it strengthens or weakens, and by whether its result needs a stronger model. Taking a broader perspective on that classification, we group the surveyed works' solutions into a few threads of concern in the baseline, namely its performance, the accountability of its validators, and the protection of exploitable information. For each thread, we identify the recurring strategies that their approaches follow. Together, these threads and strategies describe the current state of research on the Tendermint family. Where the strategies leave gaps, we pose future directions, each as an open question under an explicit fault and timing model.

### [385] [Smart Model Routing for Order-of-Magnitude LLM Cost Reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15911)
*Hesham Elbakoury,Deep Shah,Ankur Sharma*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Frontier large language models (LLMs) deliver the strongest response quality but carry per-token prices often more than an order of magnitude above those of smaller, task-adequate models. Smart model routing addresses this mismatch by assigning each query to the cheapest model expected to answer it adequately, rather than sending every request to the most capable, most expensive endpoint. This paper develops a formal cost-quality optimization framework for routing -- including a derived optimal threshold-policy structure, a calibration-versus-discrimination distinction, a cascade breakeven condition, and a sensitivity analysis over price ratio and traffic skew -- situates that framework against the principal routing architectures and the signals used to estimate query difficulty, and works through a numerical example showing how a calibrated router can reduce blended inference cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to an always-frontier deployment under specific, stated pricing and traffic assumptions, reporting both the gross reduction from routing policy alone and the net figure with the router's own overhead priced in. We situate this figure against the range reported by published routing systems (roughly 2x to frontier-level accuracy at one-fifth the cost), and close with the practical risks -- under- and over-routing, aggregate quality constraints masking segment-level harm, calibration without discrimination, calibration drift, prompt injection into routing signals, and operational failures such as tier outages and multi-provider price variation -- that determine whether the savings materialize in production. The analysis is primarily analytical, complemented by a GSM8K evaluation of the cascade framework (Section 5), validated (Section 5.2); extending the evaluation across tasks and model families is future work.

### [386] [NVIDIA Vera: A Microarchitecture-Level Comparison with Grace, Turin, and Granite Rapids](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15926)
*Joseph Moore,Thomas Green,Simon McIntosh-Smith*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: The majority of new HPC systems are centered around NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel CPUs. Vera is NVIDIA's latest data-center CPU, including its first custom data-center core design, Olympus. This paper investigates Vera in comparison to AMD Turin and Intel Granite Rapids, using NVIDIA Grace as a baseline. We navigate up the performance ladder, from microbenchmarks that isolate performance metrics, through NAS kernels and miniapps, to single-socket performance of a range of scientific codes. We find that Vera achieves the best performance of the architectures evaluated in most codes tested, and that this gain is primarily attributed to its high memory bandwidth, effective Spatial Multithreading implementation, and low-latency memory subsystem aided by the architecture's predictive structures. While Vera represents a major leap over its predecessor, we show that its comparatively modest floating-point performance trails Intel and AMD in a small number of compute-bound workloads reflecting NVIDIA's GPU focus for such workloads.

### [387] [Starscream: Reimagining LLM Sharding on AMD Instinct GPUs with GPU Partitioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15951)
*Sumanth Gudaparthi,Smeet Chheda,Ganesh Dasika*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: As GPU accelerators grow larger to meet rising compute demands, they exhibit increasingly pronounced non-uniform memory access (NUMA) characteristics that challenge existing LLM frameworks. Chiplet-based architectures provide a practical path to larger GPUs while mitigating manufacturing yield constraints. Modern GPUs such as AMD Instinct MI300X employs such a multi-die design, and further offer GPU partitioning capabilities, partitioning a single physical GPU into multiple logical devices with NUMA-aware memory domains, promising faster kernel launches, and reduced memory access latencies with improved locality. However, current parallelization strategies, designed for homogeneous GPU topologies, when applied under partitioning, extend its unidimensional sharding causing significant performance degradation. Three bottlenecks emerge: (1) memory redundancy; (2) arithmetic intensity collapse; (3) communication overhead from flat collectives. We present Starscream, a rethinking of LLM sharding for the chiplet era. Rather than stretching inter-GPU sharding thinner, Starscream adds intra-GPU sharding along an orthogonal dimension, grounded in three foundational principles: kernel shape preservation, memory redundancy elimination, and communication overhead minimization. These principles form the basis for extending any sharding strategy into the partitioning regime. We demonstrate their effectiveness using tensor parallelism as a case study. On AMD MI300X and MI355X, exploiting partitioning capabilities yields up to 4x speedup for attention and 1.43x for fused GEMMs compared to chiplet-oblivious baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of chiplet-aware designs. Starscream's principles generalize across sharding strategies and future architectures.

### [388] [Plurality Consensus for $h$-Majority via First-Repetition Rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16037)
*Niccolò D'Archivio,George Giakkoupis,Frédéric Giroire,Emanuele Natale*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: In the h-Majority dynamics, each of n agents holds one of k opinions and, in every synchronous round, observes the opinions of h agents chosen independently and uniformly at random and adopts a most frequent one among them, breaking ties uniformly at random. Let M_0 be the initial number of agents holding the most frequent opinion, and Delta_0 its bias, its lead over the second most frequent opinion. We show that, for every sample size h >= 3, if Delta_0 >= L sqrt(M_0 log n) max{1, n/(h^2 M_0)} for a sufficiently large constant L, then h-Majority reaches consensus on the initially most frequent opinion within O((1 + n/(h^2 M_0)) log n) rounds with high probability. This is the time bound proved for the DejaVu dynamics with h samples ( arXiv:2604.03648 ); our bias condition is that of DejaVu when h >= sqrt(n/M_0), and larger by a factor sqrt(n/(h^2 M_0)) otherwise. Our main contribution, the analysis of one round, rests on a comparison principle: among all rules that read the same observations and treat opinions symmetrically, plurality maximizes the difference between the probability of outputting the most frequent opinion and that of outputting any fixed competitor. We apply it to the rule that adopts the first opinion repeated among h-1 observations, and otherwise the h-th observation: its output law is the law of the new opinion of a random agent after one round of DejaVu with h-1 samples. Hence, in expectation, one round of h-Majority widens the gap between the most frequent opinion and each competitor at least as much as that round of DejaVu, whose analysis we use as a black box. Independently and concurrently, d'Amore, Rybicki, Shimizu, Shiraga and Vacus ( arXiv:2610.40562 ) obtained, among other results, the same time bound under the weaker bias condition of DejaVu, with a different analysis of one round and a martingale analysis over many rounds.

### [389] [Accelerating Distributed Variational Quantum Computing over Wireless Networks with Incentive Mechanism Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16155)
*Shaba Shaon,Dinh C. Nguyen,Octavia Dobre*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Distributed variational quantum computing (DVQC) appears as the emerging paradigm to address the limitations of near-term quantum devices by decomposing large parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) into smaller subcircuits executed across multiple quantum processors. In this context, how to incentivize quantum processors to participate actively is crucial for accelerating DVQC, yet remains largely unexplored in the literature. To address this significant gap, we propose a novel two-stage incentive framework for wireless DVQC. In the first stage, we minimize processor-side energy cost via a joint optimization of subcircuit parameters, number of noise measurements, and transmit power, efficiently solved using block coordinate descent (BCD) and successive convex approximation (SCA). In the second stage, we maximize aggregator-side system utility by selecting an optimal subset of processors based on their optimized energy costs derived from the first stage, formulating a non-convex combinatorial selection problem addressed using the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Extensive numerical experiments on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that our DVQC framework achieves training and testing performance comparable to centralized quantum computing in terms of accuracy and loss, with similar convergence behavior on MNIST and slightly slower initial convergence on CIFAR-10. Moreover, our optimization approach consistently outperforms baseline schemes in energy efficiency and system utility, revealing a strong synergy between processor-level energy minimization and incentive-driven processor selection, where reduced energy costs directly enhances a processor's likelihood of selection and contributes to higher overall system utility.

Moreover, our optimization approach consistently outperforms baseline schemes in energy efficiency and system utility, revealing a strong synergy between processor-level energy minimization and incentive-driven processor selection, where reduced energy costs directly enhances a processor's likelihood of selection and contributes to higher overall system utility.

</details>


### [390] [Fast Serverless LLM Cold Starts by Sharing and Prewarming Startup Work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16180)
*Hongjin Kim,Igjae Kim,Kwanghoon Choi,Minho Ha,Jaehyuk Huh*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: When a serverless LLM platform launches a model worker on demand, the cold start lasts roughly a minute, yet only 5-11% of it is spent loading weights. Most of the remainder goes to compilation, memory profiling and runtime setup, which each server performs again even though the outcome is identical across servers or independent of the model. We present Cairn. The server that is first to start a model publishes the weights and engine artifacts to a CXL memory pool shared across the cluster, and the remaining servers read them in place. Model-independent setup is completed ahead of time inside warm containers, and a template process replaces each container as soon as it is used. With ServerlessLLM on vLLM v0.20, six models from 1B to 14B, and two servers that share an emulated CXL pool, Cairn speeds up cold starts by 4.1-5.2x on servers without a checkpoint of their own and reduces median TTFT on a request stream by 64%.

### [391] [GC-MoE on SM120: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with Warp-Level FP8xFP4 Block-Scaled MMA on Consumer Blackwell](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16219)
*Yong Li,Haoyu Wang,Kan Liu,Tao Lan*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts decoding is latency bound: each layer serializes a token exchange, a grouped GEMM over routed experts, and a combine, while only a few tokens per rank are in flight. Prior GC-MoE fused these phases into one persistent, Green-Context-partitioned CUDA Graph on Hopper (SM90) and datacenter Blackwell (SM100). This paper rebuilds the operator for SM120 (compute capability 12.0, e.g. RTX PRO 5000) over PCIe. SM120 exposes block-scaled tensor cores only through warp-level this http URL ::mxf8f6f4: no tensor memory, no two-CTA MMA, no cluster multicast. We rebuild the kernel around a swap-AB warp-level block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights in the register A operand and FP8 activations in B, plus SM120-specific mechanisms: scale-byte selection through MMA immediates, a compact-weights path, an adaptive token-tile geometry, an expert-granular streaming dispatch with a batched bulk-pull engine and a 64-bit deduplicating pull cache, full-width BF16 returns drained by resident relay copiers over a position-major arena, and shared experts folded into the compute role. On 8xRTX PRO 5000 over PCIe the operator is 1.522x and 1.387x faster than the FlashInfer CuTe DSL W4A8 MegaMoE and the Cake MegaMoE across 18 decode points (18/18 wins each), and 1.388x faster than Cake with shared experts fused; all 94 numerical cases and 752 per-rank checks pass, at cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.

### [392] [MegaOps: A Kernel Overlapping Framework with PyTorch-like Modularity and Megakernel Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16248)
*Jinkun Lin,Byungsoo Oh,Rachee Singh*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Modern ML frameworks execute models using the kernel-per-operator paradigm, which runs each operator as a separate GPU kernel. This paradigm is modular, since developers can compose various kernel implementations and profile each kernel in isolation. However, this paradigm enforces dependencies at the granularity of entire kernels, which places a barrier between dependent kernels. These barriers cause streaming multiprocessors to idle, serialize computation and communication, and prevent a kernel from prefetching its weights while the preceding kernel runs. Megakernels remove kernel barriers by fusing the operators of an entire layer or model into a single kernel, but they give up the modularity of the kernel-per-operator paradigm. In this work, we ask whether a kernel-per-operator ML framework can perform on par with megakernels. Our key insight is that removing kernel barriers does not require fusing kernels. We develop MegaOps, a framework that launches dependent kernels on separate CUDA streams and enforces each dependency on individual tiles of the intermediate tensor that the producer kernel writes and the consumer kernel reads. Since kernels synchronize on data tiles instead of on each other's thread blocks, any two kernels that adopt the same data tiling can be composed without modifying either kernel. We evaluate MegaOps on dense Llama3 and Qwen3 models on single H100, A100, and L40 GPUs and on multi-GPU servers with 4$\times$A100 and 8$\times$H100. Our MegaOps framework matches the throughput of hand-tuned ThunderKittens megakernels, and achieves 1.09$\times$-1.10$\times$ the decode throughput and 0.98$\times$-1.10$\times$ the prefill throughput of the best-performing baseline, while reusing existing Triton, cuBLAS, and cuDNN kernels.

### [393] [Parallel Computing Systems for the Optimal Selection of Process Equipment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16290)
*Andrey B. Borisenko*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: This monograph addresses the optimal selection of equipment for chemical-engineering systems of multiproduct batch plants, a large-scale NP-hard discrete optimization problem in which, for each processing stage, a unit of standard size must be chosen so that the total capital cost of the equipment is minimized while the system remains operable and produces the required products within a given time horizon. We present the mathematical model of system operation and analyze its computational properties. We then develop a sequential branch-and-bound algorithm and its parallel versions for shared-memory systems (OpenMP), distributed-memory clusters (MPI, master-worker), and graphics processing units (CUDA), including recursive and iterative tree traversal, shared-memory optimization, and branch-divergence reduction. To overcome the exponential growth of the run time, we propose a hybrid metaheuristic in which Ant Colony Optimization finds a feasible initial solution and Simulated Annealing improves it, and we implement it on GPUs with thousands of independent threads. Finally, we propose random, constant, and multi-constant approaches to tuning the parameters of the ant colony algorithm based on statistical analysis of many parallel runs, and we study the program on GPUs of three generations and on nodes with several GPUs. Computational experiments on multi-core processors, clusters, and GPUs show that the parallel hybrid algorithm finds solutions within 0.01% of the branch-and-bound optimum in tens of seconds instead of tens of hours.

### [394] [Smoothed Analysis for Distributed MIS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16302)
*Dipan Dey,Fabien Dufoulon,William K. Moses Jr.,Gopal Pandurangan*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: We study smoothed analysis of the distributed Maximal Independent Set (MIS) problem. Luby's algorithm computes an MIS in $O(\log n)$ rounds, while the recent $\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)$ lower bound of Khoury and Schild (2026) shows that it is nearly optimal even in the LOCAL model. We ask whether small random perturbations can overcome this worst-case barrier. Given an arbitrary base graph $G$ on $n$ nodes, we consider the smoothed graph $\mathcal{G}_s=G\triangle G(n,p)$, where $G(n,p)$ is an independent random graph and $\triangle$ denotes symmetric difference. Thus, each possible edge is independently toggled with probability $p$. We establish nearly tight bounds on the smoothing needed for faster distributed MIS. For every base graph $G$, when $p=\beta\ln n/n$ for a sufficiently large constant $\beta$, a randomized LOCAL algorithm, given only $\mathcal{G}_s$, computes an MIS of $\mathcal{G}_s$ in $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ rounds with high probability. This is almost quadratically faster than the worst-case lower bound. Conversely, if $p\le(1/2-\delta)\ln n/n$ for a fixed constant $\delta>0$, there exists a base graph on which every randomized LOCAL MIS algorithm requires $\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)$ rounds on the smoothed graph. Hence, the smoothing parameter required for this speedup is optimal up to a constant factor. These results show that smoothed analysis can overcome worst-case lower-bound barriers for distributed local graph problems.

### [395] [Snoopie: A Multi-GPU Communication Profiler and Visualizer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16330)
*Mohammad Kefah Taha Issa,Muhammad Aditya Sasongko,Ilyas Turimbetov,Javid Baydamirli,Doğan Sağbili,Didem Unat*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: With data movement becoming one of the most expensive bottlenecks in computing, the need for profiling tools to analyze communication becomes crucial for effectively scaling multi-GPU applications. While existing profiling tools including first-party software by GPU vendors are robust and excel at capturing compute operations within a single GPU, support for monitoring GPU-GPU data transfers and calls issued by communication libraries is currently inadequate. To fill these gaps, we introduce Snoopie, an instrumentation-based multi-GPU communication profiling tool built on NVBit, capable of tracking peer-to-peer transfers and GPU-centric communication library calls. To increase programmer productivity, Snoopie can attribute data movement to the source code line and the data objects involved. It comes with multiple visualization modes at varying granularities, from a coarse view of the data movement in the system as a whole to specific instructions and addresses. Our case studies demonstrate Snoopie's effectiveness in monitoring data movement, locating performance bugs in applications, and understanding concrete data transfers abstracted beneath communication libraries. The tool is publicly available at this https URL .

### [396] [SS-HSDP: Efficient and Flexible Sharded Data Parallelism via Runtime-Update Decoupling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16467)
*Chendong Xiang,Pengle Zhang,Jinliang Li,Zichen Liang,Jintao Zhang,Fan Bao,Jun Zhu,Jianfei Chen*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Sharded data parallelism enables memory-efficient training of large models. While efficient training kernels favor packed, kernel-specific data layouts, optimizers may require variant data structures as optimization units. Existing sharded data-parallel frameworks couple these two choices, limiting runtime efficiency and optimization flexibility. To address this, we present \textbf{\our}, a training framework that separates runtime parameters from update parameters, allowing computation layouts and optimization units to be organized independently. Through shared data views and hierarchical sharding, \our supports this separation while avoiding redundant data movement. This design supports a broad range of optimizers, including matrix-based methods such as Muon, and performance optimizations such as fully zero-copy execution. Experiments on video and language model workloads with MXFP8 training show that \our achieves higher Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) than FSDP2, veScale-FSDP, and Megatron-FSDP. At 128 GPUs, MFU improves by up to 21.7\% over the fastest evaluated baseline, with comparable or lower peak memory usage.

### [397] [Autonomous Mobile Robots on a Computing Field](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16652)
*Yonghwan Kim,Gil-Tak Kong,Un-Sook Choi*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: We introduce CABOT, a computational model for autonomous mobile robots in which the discrete plane the robots operate on is not a passive stage but an active computing medium. In the classical Look-Compute-Move (LCM) model every increase in computational capability is obtained by strengthening the robots themselves, with lights, memory or wider visibility, at a cost paid once per robot. CABOT strengthens the environment instead: each cell of the grid holds a state from a finite set Q, the states evolve synchronously under a uniform local rule that also senses whether a robot stands on the cell, that is, the floor is a cellular automaton, and the Look operation returns the states of the visible cells in addition to the positions of the visible robots. The robots are as weak as we can make them: oblivious, silent, lightless, myopic with visibility range 1, without multiplicity detection and unable to write to the floor. The number of field states |Q|, rather than any robot capability, becomes the measure of the resources required. On an inert floor (|Q| = 1) such robots can neither form a line, nor gather from scattered positions, nor explore a grid. We show that a handful of states changes this. Line Formation from connected configurations is solvable with four states, and field-silently, so that the floor also reaches a fixed point, with five. Gathering from arbitrary, possibly disconnected, configurations is solvable with three states and Line Formation from arbitrary configurations with six; we prove that neither can be solved field-silently with any number of states. A single robot explores every finite grid forever with four states and every torus with two, which is optimal. Further rule sets, validated by simulation only, equalize the spacing of robots on a row, fill a pattern painted on the floor and guide robots through a maze, and indicate the range of the model.

### [398] [Locality Meets Interference: Structure and Scheduling in Radio Multicasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16844)
*Qin Xin*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: We study multipoint-to-multipoint multicasting in synchronous radio networks with unknown participant locations and unrestricted message aggregation. Let $n$ be the network size, $k$ the number of participants, and $d$ their hop diameter. A supplied distance-two coloring with $C$ colors yields completion within $(C-1)d+1$ slots and at most $nk$ transmissions. In unit disk graphs, coordinates, one-hop neighbor data, and a common degree bound $\Delta_0$ suffice for a $15(\Delta_0+1)$-color schedule. A known fixed separation bound permits optimal deterministic $\Theta(d)$ completion from coordinates alone. Without geometric data, strong selectivity gives $O(d\min\{n,(\Delta_0+1)^2\log n\})$ slots when $n$ is known. Independent random transmission gives $O((\Delta_0+1)(d+\log(k/\eta)))$ slots with failure probability at most $\eta$; for fixed $\Delta_0$, this simplifies to $O(d+\log(1/\eta))$. A star construction shows that the logarithmic term is necessary for this random rule when the degree grows. We extend color schedules to fixed deletions and subgraphs connected over bounded windows of cycles. Separate conditional reductions preserve additive costs under diameter guessing and control parameter-table and cluster preprocessing. Finally, a counterexample shows that pruning and reranking a breadth-first tree can destroy interference-free delivery. For one-hop designated delivery with receiver degree at most $b$, we prove that the optimal schedule length equals the chromatic number of an associated conflict graph and is at most $2b-1$, with matching examples.

### [399] [PACER: GPU Excursion Management for ML Workloads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17206)
*Rutwik Jain,Nathaniel Morris,Yiwei Jiang,Shidhartha Das,Gary Kao,Indrani Paul,Shivaram Venkataraman,Srilatha Manne,Matthew D. Sinclair*

Main category: cs.DC

TL;DR: Variability is an inherent characteristic of modern GPU systems, arising from a combination of process variation, dynamic environmental conditions, and power management decisions. Prior work has characterized inter-GPU variability and found consistent performance differences across GPUs. However, we observe that modern workloads, particularly large language models (LLMs), exhibit significant intra-GPU variability. Their short-running kernels interact poorly with the coarse granularity of dynamic power management mechanisms, leading to unpredictable performance. A key source of this intra-GPU transient variability is power excursions, also referred to as electrical design power peaks (EDP$_{p}$), where power temporarily exceeds the GPU's rated power limits. While power management mechanisms are designed to ensure reliable operation despite the presence of EDP$_{p}$ sustained power peaks cause throttling that detrimentally impacts overall application performance. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to characterize the magnitude and frequency of EDP$_{p}$, showing that frequent, significant power overshoots are especially common in ML workloads, which combine high power draw, short kernels, and rapidly changing compute demands. To address this, we design and leverage hardware and firmware mechanisms to provide consistent power management behavior that reduces intra-GPU variability due to EDP$_{p}$ and improves overall performance. We evaluate our techniques across a range of popular workloads. Our approach improves performance by 3-12% over state-of-the-art GPU power management and comes within 3% of an oracular solution.

However, we observe that modern workloads, particularly large language models (LLMs), exhibit significant intra-GPU variability. Their short-running kernels interact poorly with the coarse granularity of dynamic power management mechanisms, leading to unpredictable performance. A key source of this intra-GPU transient variability is power excursions, also referred to as electrical design power peaks (EDP$_{p}$), where power temporarily exceeds the GPU's rated power limits. While power management mechanisms are designed to ensure reliable operation despite the presence of EDP$_{p}$ sustained power peaks cause throttling that detrimentally impacts overall application performance. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to characterize the magnitude and frequency of EDP$_{p}$, showing that frequent, significant power overshoots are especially common in ML workloads, which combine high power draw, short kernels, and rapidly changing compute demands. To address this, we design and leverage hardware and firmware mechanisms to provide consistent power management behavior that reduces intra-GPU variability due to EDP$_{p}$ and improves overall performance. We evaluate our techniques across a range of popular workloads. Our approach improves performance by 3-12% over state-of-the-art GPU power management and comes within 3% of an oracular solution.

</details>

### [400] [Tideway: Phase-Aware Tiered Memory Management for MoE Inference on Consumer Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14848)
*Yifei Wang,Tsun-yu Yang,Yechen Xu,Hancheng Ye,Qinsi Wang,Baijun Zhou,Tingjun Chen,Hai "Helen" Li,Danyang Zhuo,Yiran Chen*

Main category: cs.OS

TL;DR: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly becoming a dominant paradigm for AI applications. Recently, there is a growing demand to deploy large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models locally on consumer PCs to balance data privacy, API costs, and inference efficiency. However, unlike datacenter servers with abundant DRAM, consumer devices are tightly constrained in both GPU VRAM and host RAM, forcing massive MoE weights to spill across VRAM, host RAM, and SSD. Under such spilling, we observe that existing systems fail to fully utilize this memory hierarchy, treating the tiers as independent caches and thrashing in inference. We present TIDEWAY, a system for efficient inference of large MoE models on memory-constrained consumer devices. Our core insight is to manage host RAM and GPU VRAM as a unified memory pool. Within this pool, TIDEWAY couples phase-aware memory layouts, which adapt to the distinct access patterns of prefill and decode, with an execution engine that optimizes CUDA Graph execution under expert paging. Our evaluations on representative consumer hardware with frontier MoE models demonstrate that TIDEWAY significantly outperforms state-of-the-art systems. On average, TIDEWAY achieves speedups of 1.97x in end-to-end latency and 2.40x in Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), along with 1.61x higher decode throughput against the fastest baseline. Our source code is publicly available at this https URL .

  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI enhancement unavailable (ai_circuit_open). Original arXiv metadata is preserved.

Method: AI enhancement unavailable; see the original abstract.

Result: AI enhancement unavailable; see the original abstract.

Conclusion: AI enhancement unavailable (ai_circuit_open). Original arXiv metadata is preserved.

However, unlike datacenter servers with abundant DRAM, consumer devices are tightly constrained in both GPU VRAM and host RAM, forcing massive MoE weights to spill across VRAM, host RAM, and SSD. Under such spilling, we observe that existing systems fail to fully utilize this memory hierarchy, treating the tiers as independent caches and thrashing in inference. We present TIDEWAY, a system for efficient inference of large MoE models on memory-constrained consumer devices. Our core insight is to manage host RAM and GPU VRAM as a unified memory pool. Within this pool, TIDEWAY couples phase-aware memory layouts, which adapt to the distinct access patterns of prefill and decode, with an execution engine that optimizes CUDA Graph execution under expert paging. Our evaluations on representative consumer hardware with frontier MoE models demonstrate that TIDEWAY significantly outperforms state-of-the-art systems. On average, TIDEWAY achieves speedups of 1.97x in end-to-end latency and 2.40x in Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), along with 1.61x higher decode throughput against the fastest baseline.
